beats.text: Welcome. This video is about the first hours of an infection. The exam asks you to compare innate and adaptive immunity, name the barrier molecules, and place each phase on a time line.
beats.no_facts_reason: Intro and exam hook; no factual claim.
beats.visual: Title card, then three exam goals appear.

beats.text: Innate immunity is fully functional before an infection occurs. It gives continuous barrier defense. It reacts to microbes in the first hours or days, before adaptive responses develop.
beats.visual: Shield labelled INNATE appears at once; clock shows hours.

beats.text: Adaptive immunity needs exposure to the microbe. Lymphocyte activation and differentiation take several days. So the adaptive response is slow, and innate immunity must protect first.
beats.visual: ADAPTIVE lymphocyte appears on the right with a 'days' tag.

beats.text: Now let's compare the two branches side by side. First, specificity. Innate immunity recognizes molecules shared by groups of related microbes, and molecules from damaged host cells. That is only about one thousand products. Adaptive immunity can recognize millions of antigens.
beats.visual: D1 table: row 'Recognizes' — ~1000 vs millions.

beats.text: Next, receptors. Innate immunity uses germline-encoded, invariant receptors, and there are fewer than one hundred types. Adaptive immunity uses only two receptor types, immunoglobulin and the T-cell receptor. Each has millions of variants from somatically rearranged genes.
beats.visual: D1 table: row 'Receptors' — germline <100 vs Ig + TCR, rearranged.

beats.text: Innate receptors are nonclonal. All cells of one lineage carry the same receptors. Adaptive receptors are clonal.
beats.visual: D1 table: row 'Distribution' — nonclonal vs clonal, with mini cells.

beats.text: Innate immunity has limited memory. A repeat exposure usually gives the same kinetics, magnitude and quality as the first response. Adaptive immunity has memory. Secondary adaptive responses are usually faster and greater.
beats.visual: D1 table: row 'Memory' — limited vs yes; two response bumps.

beats.text: Neither branch normally reacts against self. Innate immunity ignores healthy cells for three reasons. Normal cells lack most ligands, the receptors sit in separate compartments, and regulatory proteins block activation.
beats.visual: D1 table: row 'Self' — no vs no; then three reasons list.

beats.text: So what does innate immunity actually see? Molecules shared by classes of microbes are called pathogen-associated molecular patterns, or PAMPs. They are often essential for microbial survival. So microbes usually cannot evade innate immunity by losing them.
beats.say: So what does innate immunity actually see? Molecules shared by classes of microbes are called pathogen-associated molecular patterns, or pamps. They are often essential for microbial survival. So microbes usually cannot evade innate immunity by losing them.
beats.visual: Microbe with PAMP spikes; receptor on a cell binds them.

beats.text: Damaged or dying host cells release damage-associated molecular patterns, or DAMPs. DAMPs also signal sterile injury, such as burns or trauma. Cells that die by apoptosis generally do not release DAMPs. Some DAMP cytokines are called alarmins.
beats.say: Damaged or dying host cells release damage-associated molecular patterns, or damps. Damps also signal sterile injury, such as burns or trauma. Cells that die by apoptosis generally do not release damps. Some damp cytokines are called alarmins.
beats.visual: Burst host cell releases DAMPs; apoptotic cell releases none (crossed).

beats.text: Now to the front line. The main interfaces with the environment are the skin and the mucosa of the gut, the airways and the genitourinary tract. Surface epithelia give three types of barrier: mechanical, chemical and microbiological.
beats.visual: D2: epithelial layer drawn; three barrier labels appear.

beats.text: Think of it like a castle. The wall is the physical barrier. Boiling oil from the wall is the chemical barrier. Friendly tenants who fill every room are the microbiota.
beats.no_facts_reason: Flagged analogy (from the M1 module analogy box); restates b11.
beats.visual: Castle sketch: wall, oil pot, tenants.

beats.text: First, the physical barrier. Epithelial cells form tight junctions that block microbes between the cells. In the skin, the outer keratin layer blocks penetration. Skin infections usually occur after a barrier breach.
beats.visual: D2 zoom: cells with tight junctions; microbe bounces off.

beats.text: Mucosal epithelia produce mucus, which contains mucins and impairs microbial invasion. In the airways, goblet cells secrete mucus, and beating cilia move it outward. In the gut, peristalsis helps to remove microbes.
beats.visual: Mucus layer and cilia on top of cells; arrow shows outward flow.

beats.text: Here is the clinical link. In cystic fibrosis, thick mucus or impaired ciliary movement leads to lung infections. The bacteria colonize the epithelial surface but do not cross it. Failure of peristalsis typically leads to bacterial overgrowth in the gut lumen.
beats.visual: Pink 'Cystic fibrosis' box: thick mucus, bacteria sit on top.

beats.text: Second, the chemical barrier. In the upper gut, stomach acid, digestive enzymes and bile salts act together. Tears and saliva contain lysozyme, which cleaves peptidoglycan. Lysozyme works better against Gram-positive bacteria, because an LPS outer layer covers the peptidoglycan of Gram-negative bacteria.
beats.say: Second, the chemical barrier. In the upper gut, stomach acid, digestive enzymes and bile salts act together. Tears and saliva contain lysozyme, which cleaves peptidoglycan. Lysozyme works better against Gram-positive bacteria, because an L P S outer layer covers the peptidoglycan of Gram-negative bacteria.
beats.visual: Lysozyme scissors cut a Gram+ wall; Gram- wall shielded by LPS.

beats.text: Mammals have three important classes of antimicrobial peptides: defensins, cathelicidins and histatins. Defensins are small cationic peptides. Within minutes, they disrupt the membranes of bacteria, fungi and some enveloped viruses.
beats.visual: Three peptide labels; defensins punch holes in a membrane.

beats.text: Paneth cells in the small-bowel crypts are a major source of alpha-defensins. Beta-defensins come mainly from the airway, urogenital tract, skin and tongue. Cathelicidin gives LL-37, which binds and neutralizes LPS. Histatins from the salivary glands act against Candida albicans.
beats.say: Paneth cells in the small-bowel crypts are a major source of alpha defensins. Beta defensins come mainly from the airway, urogenital tract, skin and tongue. Cathelicidin gives L L 37, which binds and neutralizes L P S. Histatins from the salivary glands act against Candida albicans.
beats.visual: Source table: molecule → source → key fact.

beats.text: Third, the microbiological barrier. Commensal microbes compete with pathogens for nutrients and attachment sites. They make antimicrobial substances, such as lactic acid from vaginal lactobacilli. They also stimulate epithelial cells to make antimicrobial peptides.
beats.visual: Green commensals cover the surface; pathogen finds no space.

beats.text: When antibiotics kill commensals, pathogens frequently replace them and cause disease. And beneath all epithelial surfaces, phagocytes wait to engulf any microbe that gets through.
beats.visual: Antibiotic wipes commensals; pink pathogen takes over; phagocyte below.

beats.text: Now let's put everything on a time line. The response to a new pathogen has three phases. Phase one is the immediate innate phase, from zero to four hours. Preformed soluble molecules act at once: lysozyme, defensins and complement.
beats.visual: D3 timeline axis; 0-4 h block fills with preformed molecules.

beats.text: Phase two is the early induced innate phase, from four to ninety-six hours. Innate cells recognize PAMPs and become activated. An inflammatory response often first counters the spread of the pathogen.
beats.say: Phase two is the early induced innate phase, from four to ninety-six hours. Innate cells recognize pamps and become activated. An inflammatory response often first counters the spread of the pathogen.
beats.visual: D3: 4-96 h block; activated cell + inflammation.

beats.text: During this phase, dendritic cells carry antigen to local lymphoid tissue. Phase three, the adaptive phase, starts after ninety-six hours. It is late because rare specific B and T cells must first expand clonally.
beats.visual: D3: >96 h block; one lymphocyte multiplies into a clone.

beats.text: Innate defenses act within minutes. An adaptive response is necessary only when innate defenses are bypassed, evaded or overwhelmed. Even then, innate immunity keeps pathogen numbers in check. The phase boundaries are approximate and vary between infections.
beats.visual: Pathogen curve held down by innate; boundaries go fuzzy.

beats.text: The two branches work together. The innate response gives early danger signals that start adaptive responses. In turn, adaptive responses often make innate mechanisms stronger.
beats.visual: Two-way arrow between INNATE and ADAPTIVE.

beats.text: Five things to remember. One: innate immunity is fully functional before infection and has limited memory. Two: it uses fewer than one hundred germline-encoded, nonclonal receptor types. Three: epithelia give mechanical, chemical and microbiological barriers.
beats.visual: Recap list items 1-3.

beats.text: Four: key barrier molecules are lysozyme, defensins, cathelicidin and histatins. Five: the three phases are zero to four hours, four to ninety-six hours, and after ninety-six hours.
beats.visual: Recap list items 4-5.

beats.text: And one exam trap. Lysozyme is more effective against Gram-positive bacteria, not Gram-negative bacteria. The LPS outer layer of Gram-negative bacteria covers the peptidoglycan.
beats.say: And one exam trap. Lysozyme is more effective against Gram-positive bacteria, not Gram-negative bacteria. The L P S outer layer of Gram-negative bacteria covers the peptidoglycan.
beats.visual: TRAP card: Gram+ ✓ / Gram− ✗ for lysozyme.

beats.text: Next: the cells of innate immunity. We meet the phagocytes, dendritic cells, NK cells, mast cells, eosinophils and innate lymphoid cells.
beats.say: Next: the cells of innate immunity. We meet the phagocytes, dendritic cells, N K cells, mast cells, eosinophils and innate lymphoid cells.
beats.visual: Row of cartoon cells; 'Next: V2' card.
